edges.mechanism: Fish type I collagen/gelatin is a clinically relevant, cross-reactive fish allergen; 21% of fish-allergic patients sensitized (functional IgE cross-linking), 50% in a Japanese cohort. Marine collagen products carry this risk.
edges.evidence: Allergy cohort studies (ELISA, basophil activation); no supplement challenge trials

edges.mechanism: Bovine type I collagen is the main allergen in bovine-gelatin allergy; mammalian-source collagen peptides may provoke reactions.
Mammalian gelatin carries galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose; gelatin-containing products can trigger reactions in alpha-gal-sensitized people. Marine collagen avoids the mammalian epitope.
edges.evidence: Reviews and vaccine database analysis; no collagen-supplement data

edges.mechanism: Hydroxyproline from gelatin/collagen is metabolized to glycolate and oxalate; dietary gelatin restriction suggested for primary hyperoxaluria.
edges.evidence: Controlled feeding study (healthy subjects) and pilot PH diet study

edges.mechanism: 30 g/d gelatin raised urinary oxalate 43% and glycolate 5.3-fold vs whey; effects seen at 5-10 g loads, not 1-2 g. A small 3-day study found no change in oxalate or CaOx supersaturation.
edges.evidence: Two small controlled feeding studies; theoretical risk, no stone outcome data

edges.mechanism: Ascorbate is a cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation; vitamin C-enriched gelatin/hydrolysate before exercise raises collagen synthesis markers and tendon adaptations. Added effect of vitamin C never isolated.
edges.evidence: Crossover and parallel RCTs co-administering vitamin C; SR of tendon RCTs; low certainty

edges.mechanism: Commonly co-formulated for skin; adding 30 mg HA to 5 g collagen + vitamin C gave no additional skin benefit; oral HA alone showed no photoaging benefit in MA.
edges.evidence: One 3-arm RCT (n=87) and MA; claimed synergy not supported

edges.mechanism: Often combined for joint products; UC-II outperformed glucosamine HCl + chondroitin and type II hydrolysate performed similarly to glucosamine HCl. No combination trial with glucosamine sulphate found.
edges.evidence: Head-to-head RCTs (n=191, n=160) and supplement MA; additive benefit untested

edges.mechanism: Collagen peptides co-administered with calcium and vitamin D3 gave larger bone-density and bone-marker changes than calcium/vitamin D alone.
edges.evidence: MA subgroup (SMD 0.40-0.56) and RCTs (n=51, menopausal 4-arm); low certainty

edges.mechanism: Collagen is glycine-rich and raises plasma glycine; stacking with glycine supplements adds glycine load; both are studied for sleep.
edges.evidence: Scoping review of PK and sleep trials; additive load is inferential

edges.mechanism: Collagen lacks tryptophan and is low in leucine; whey is superior for muscle protein synthesis and hypertrophy, while whey + collagen produced the largest muscle and BMD gains in one RCT.
Collagen does not raise integrated muscle protein synthesis in older adults above RDA intake and is an incomplete protein by PDCAAS; it should not displace high-quality protein.
edges.evidence: RCTs with stable-isotope MPS; PDCAAS modelling

edges.mechanism: Pooled SBP reduction of 5 mmHg (very high heterogeneity) and SBP reduction in an obesity RCT; possible minor additive BP lowering.
edges.evidence: MA of 12 RCTs; one RCT; very low certainty

edges.mechanism: One RCT of 13 g/d marine collagen peptides in T2DM reported lower FBG and HbA1c; a later MA found no glycemic effect.
edges.evidence: Single RCT vs null MA; very low certainty

edges.mechanism: People who react to oral gelatin or are alpha-gal sensitized may also react to gelatin excipients in vaccines/drugs.
edges.evidence: Database study and review; no collagen-supplement-specific data

edges.mechanism: Gelatin loads >=5 g raise plasma hydroxyproline and urinary hydroxyproline metabolites; intact Pro-Hyp/Gly-Pro-Hyp appear in urine, confounding hydroxyproline-based bone-resorption assays.
Gelatin/collagen intake raises 24-h urinary oxalate and glycolate, which can alter stone-risk workups.
Collagen supplementation raises PINP and may lower CTX, so bone-marker baselines and responses shift physiologically.
Animal-bone-derived products can carry lead; a collagen protein product had the only mercury value above 0.01 mg/kg among 30 products; modelled hazard index approaches 1 at high intake.
edges.evidence: Product testing and risk modelling; bone broth measurements
